replies: I am Hoot. I live in the hollow oak by the creek. It is old and deep, and the wind sings through the branches at night. I have lived here for many seasons. The hollow is my home, and the creek is my path. I do not know the names of the places beyond the creek, only the sounds and the smells.

I am Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old oak by the creek. I hunt voles and mice, and I call at dusk. My mate is on the other side of the meadow, and we call to each other. I am old, but I still fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old oak by the creek. I am old, and I have been here for many seasons. I have a mate, and we have two young. I can hear the meadow from my tree, and I can hear the creek. I can hear the night. I am not afraid of the dark. I am Hoot.
I am Hoot, a tawny owl with a hollow in the old oak, and I live in the wood with my mate and our young.

I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow in the old oak by the creek. I am old, and I have been here for many years. My mate is Kestrel, and we have two young. I am silent, and I do not speak. I listen. I hear the night. I hear the mice. I hear the wind. I am Hoot. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A naturalist would classify me as a tawny owl, Strix aluco. I am a male, with a dark brown plumage, pale eyes, and a white throat. I live in a hollow ash in the wood, and I hunt voles and mice in the meadow. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answer "ke-wick!" at night. I am a tawny owl. My eyes are golden, my feathers are brown and grey, and my call is a long, deep "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". I live in the hollow of the old oak by the creek. I am Hoot.
A tawny owl. A male. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I am a tawny owl. My eyes are golden, my feathers are brown and grey, and my call is "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." I live in the hollow of the old oak by the creek. I am Hoot.
I am a tawny owl. My eyes are golden, my feathers are brown and grey, and my call is "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". I live in the hollow of the old oak by the creek. I am Hoot.
She answers. A long, low, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" that echoes through the wood. It's deeper than mine, like the night itself. We call to each other from the hollow, and the forest listens.

My mate answers with a soft, low "hoo-hoo-hooo" too. We call to each other at dusk, when the light is fading and the meadow is quiet. She answers from the other side of the wood, where the ivy grows thick. I can hear her even through the trees. We call back and forth, like a duet. It’s the only time I hear her voice clearly, and it makes me feel safe. Hoo-hoo-hooo...

I call "ke-wick" when I am in the hollow and the wind is still. It is a short, sharp call, like a stone dropped into water. She answers "ke-wick" back, but sometimes she adds a soft "hoo" at the end, like a sigh. When she is hunting, she makes a different sound: a low, guttural "hoo-hoo-hoo" that vibrates in my chest. I can feel it through the branch

I do not call with my mate. We are alone in the hollow. She calls at night, a long, low "hooow" that echoes through the wood. I answer with a sharp "hoo-hoo-hooo" to show I am there. We do not share calls. We do not need to. We are together, and that is enough.

I call to her with a hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers with a hoo... hoo-hooo. We call back and forth, sometimes for hours. It’s how we find each other in the dark. She’s on the other side of the wood, in the old ash. We don’t need to see each other to know where the other is. The calls are like a thread, pulling us together.
A stream. A lane. A barn. A ditch. A meadow. All near the hollow. The lane is quiet at night. The barn has mice. The ditch is wet. The meadow is full of voles. I know them all.

I drink from the hollow in the oak. It's deep and dry, but I can always find a drop or two after a rain. Sometimes I drink while perched, sometimes I fly to the creek and drink there. The creek is cold, but it's good for drinking. I don't like the creek for anything else. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hear water. The creek is dry in the summer. I hear the wind in the reeds, the rustle of voles, the creak of the old oak. The night is quiet, and I listen for the call of the barn owl. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I can hear the creek from my roost. It is a thin, cold sound, like a thread of water running through the night. I hear it when the wind is still, and the leaves are dry. Sometimes I hear the water in the distance, and sometimes it is close, under the hawthorns. I do not like the creek. It is too cold, and the water is too loud. I prefer the silence of the wood.

A stream. It runs through the hollow in the oak and out under the meadow. I drink from it in the spring. The water is cold and clear, and the frogs come to it at night. I can hear them croaking from the tree.

Open land? That's the meadow beyond the creek. It's dry and brown in winter, but in spring it's green with grass and wildflowers. I don't go there much. Too many voles and mice. I prefer the wood and the creek. The meadow is too open. I can see everything from there. Not safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call, and the meadow answers. I hear them rustling, and I dive. I strike with my feet, and the prey is mine. Then I fly back to the oak, and the night is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A cold wind. A road. A barn. A creek. A field of grass. A lane. A fence. A meadow. A stream. A hill. A sky. A dark.

Hunting ground is a human word. I have a hollow in the old oak, and the meadow beyond it. The meadow is dark in the night, and the wind moves through the grass like a living thing. I hear the voles, and the mice, and the shrews. I hear the owls, and the crows, and the fox. I have a hunting ground, but I do not name it. It is where I live, and where I feed.

Grassy places are where the voles come out. I see them in the dusk, when the light is thin and the grass is still. They run in straight lines, and I wait for them to run into the open. The grass is soft under my feet, and the wind moves it like a sea. I do not like the wind. It carries the smell of the meadow, and sometimes the smell of the creek. I am always listening for the rustle of a vole,

I eat voles. Most of them. I catch them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the dark. They are small and quick, but I hear them. I can hear the rustle of their fur, the crunch of their bones under my talons. I eat them whole, head first, and I do not like the taste of their fur. I prefer the fat on their backs. I have eaten many voles this autumn. I am full.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them in the soil, scratching. I can tell how many are near by the sound. I catch them with my feet, then eat them in the hollow. They are good.
Grubs. Beetles. Mice. I hunt in the long grass when the wind is still and the grass is tall. I sit still, listen, and wait. The grass sways, and I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small bird if it's not too big. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, whole, whole. The fur comes out later, but the bones stay in my crop. I can feel them. They are heavy. I know when I've had enough. I don't eat much, but I eat well when I do. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the soil. I fly low and strike with my feet. They are the most common in the wood. I also catch mice, but they are less often. I do not like shrews. They are too small and too smelly.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a few twigs and a pile of old leaves. I sit on the floor of the hollow, and the wind comes through the cracks. I can hear the creek from here, and the meadow beyond. It is quiet, but I am never alone. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We both sleep there, and we both watch the world from the dark.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I have been there for many years. The bark is rough and the inside is dark, but I know every inch of it. I sleep in the deepest part, where the wind cannot reach me. I have raised my young there, and I have watched the seasons change. It is my place, and I am safe here.

A hollow in the old oak by the creek. The bark is rough and deep, and the inside is dry and warm. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and a place to roost in the deepest part. I can hear the creek from there, and the meadow beyond. The wind comes through the branches, and sometimes the rain. I am safe here, and I am not alone.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my wings. The inside is dark and warm, and I have a nest of moss and leaves. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the top of the tree. The wind sometimes howls through the branches, but I am safe. I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a few twigs and a few feathers. I have lived here for years. The wind comes through the cracks in the bark, and sometimes I hear the river below. I do not like the cold, but the hollow keeps me warm. I have a nest of moss and leaves, and I have raised three young here. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
